stated: Reform UK will raise the National Insurance rate to 20% for foreign workers, exempting essential foreign health and care workers and businesses with 5 or fewer staff, to incentivise employing British citizens and boost wages.

source.quote: Employer Immigration Tax The National Insurance rate will be raised to 20% for foreign workers. This would incentivise businesses to employ British citizens whose National Insurance rate would stay at 13.8%. Essential foreign health and care workers would be exempt from the tax, as would businesses who employ 5 staff members and under.

bearing_set.reason: The policy directly targets wage levels and employment patterns by raising employer NI costs for foreign workers, with the explicit goal of shifting hiring toward British workers and boosting their wages — a material, non-negligible verdict on pay and job quality is unavoidable.

Raising employer NI to 20% for a significant portion of the workforce increases business labour costs, which are plausibly passed through to consumer prices (cost-push inflation), and the wage effects on different household types create a real, scoreable impact on real disposable income and the cost of essentials.

The policy creates a statutory differential employer-NI rate based solely on worker national origin, which bears directly on equal-treatment and anti-discrimination indicators in the employment relationship for foreign workers.

Raising employer NI to 20% for foreign workers (outside exemptions) generates additional tax revenue, but the net fiscal effect is contested since the stated intent is behavioural change that would shrink the new tax base — a real and non-negligible bearing on public finances sustainability.

Higher employer costs for foreign labour raise business operating costs in sectors relying on non-exempt international workers, plausibly reducing business investment, competitiveness, and productivity — a concrete macro mechanism on aggregate living standards.

membership_note: Four fundamentals bear non-negligibly: O4 (primary design target — wage and employment distribution), O9 (statutory differential treatment by national origin), O12 (revenue and fiscal impact), O13 (employer-cost effects on productivity and investment). O11 is excluded because this is an employer-side tax, not a direct change to household take-home pay; wage pass-through is captured under O4. O14 is excluded because the primary redistribution is between British and foreign workers rather than between rich and poor, and the Gini mechanism is too indirect to clear the non-negligible bar without a more specific model.
